Clear /dev/shm before process startup to prevent crashloops (#364)

When vLLM crashes there is no guarantee that /dev/shm will
be cleaned up. Since we are the only consumer of the volume
ensure it is empty before the process starts. Otherwise we
may run out of shm for NCCL init during subsequent crashes
converting temporary crashes to a permanent one.

Fixes issue #352

* feat: Add comprehensive readiness probe for vLLM containers

Implements model-aware health checking for Kubernetes readiness probes.
Ensures pods are marked Ready only when vLLM has loaded models and
API is serving requests, preventing premature traffic routing.

Changes:
- Add readiness_probe.sh script with /health and /v1/models validation
- Update Dockerfiles to include probe script in images
- Update example configurations with exec probes
- Add mandatory PORT parameter to prevent misconfigurations
- Add documentation for probe usage

Tested with simulated accelerator deployment on Kind cluster.

Closes #300

Signed-off-by: rajinator <rajx360@gmail.com>

* refactor: Pivot from exec to HTTP probes for model-aware readiness

Based on PR #330 reviewer feedback, this commit changes the readiness
checking approach from exec-based scripts to native HTTP probes using
vLLM's OpenAI-compatible API endpoints.

**Why This Change:**

Exec probes have significant drawbacks:
- Higher overhead (fork/exec on every probe)
- Incompatible with many cloud load balancers
- More complex to debug and maintain
- Requires custom scripts in container images

HTTP probes using /v1/models provide the same model-aware readiness
checking with better cloud integration and lower overhead.

**Changes:**

Container Images:
- Remove readiness_probe.sh script
- Remove script installation from all Dockerfiles (cuda, aws, xpu)

Example Configurations:
- Update simulated-accelerators values.yaml to HTTP probes
- Update wide-ep-lws manifests (decode.yaml, prefill.yaml) to HTTP probes
- Update .gitignore to exclude test artifacts

Documentation:
- Rewrite docs/readiness-probes.md to recommend HTTP probe strategy
- Document /v1/models endpoint for model-aware readiness
- Document /health endpoint for liveness checks

**Probe Strategy:**

```yaml
startupProbe:  # Model loading during initialization
  httpGet:
    path: /v1/models
    port: 8000

livenessProbe:  # Server process health
  httpGet:
    path: /health
    port: 8000

readinessProbe:  # Model ready to serve
  httpGet:
    path: /v1/models
    port: 8000
```

Tested with 3-node Kind cluster running simulated accelerators.
All decode (3 replicas) and prefill (1 replica) pods reached Ready
state with no probe failures.

Related: #300
Addresses: PR #330 feedback from @smarterclayton

Signed-off-by: rajinator <rajx360@gmail.com>

Patch nvshmem to avoid an uninitialized value passed to RoCE (#407)

NVSHMEM does not clear a stack allocated struct `ibv_ah_attr`
which is passed directly to the kernel RDMA functions. On
kernels with a patch to validate the value of static_rate
the create_ah() function will return EINVAL (sometimes).

When built in environments that automatically zero stack
values, the library will always initialize the device to
the default rate. Otherwise, it may result in the error

`Unable to create ah.` especially on RoCE devices.

guides: Make vLLM log more useful in inference-scheduling (#439)

This change makes the vLLM logging more user friendly out of the box
for someone using this example to try out llm-d.

- `--disable-uvicorn-access-log`

This disables logging every HTTP request received by vLLM. When this
is on, the log is flooded with many requests to `/metrics` every
second. To disable this message only for the `/metrics`, we could use
a custom logger configuraiton, but it would probably double the size
of this example, so I'm not sure it's worth it.

- Change `VLLM_LOGGING_LEVEL` from `DEBUG` to `INFO`

It's nice to have this in the log to make it easy to change quickly,
but the `DEBUG` logs are a bit much for a typical user. The env var is
still in place to make it very easy to change if someone needs to for
debugging something.

fix: EPP configuration issues in precise-prefix-cache-aware guide (#512)

* fix: EPP configuration issues in precise-prefix-cache-aware guide

This patch fixes two issues in the precise-prefix-cache-aware guide that
cause EPP (Endpoint Picker) deployment failures:

**Problem**: The `flags` field format is not correctly processed by the
inferencepool Helm chart, causing EPP to crash on startup.

**Error log**:
```
flag provided but not defined: -0
Usage of /epp:
  -alsologtostderr
        log to standard error as well as files
  ...
```

**Root cause**: The Helm chart converts `flags: [{name: v, value: 4}]` to
an invalid argument `--0 map[name:v value:4]` instead of `-v=4`.

**Fix**: Change `flags` to `extraArgs` with the correct format "-v=4".

**Problem**: When EPP initializes the precise-prefix-cache-scorer plugin,
it attempts to download the HuggingFace tokenizer to a read-only directory.

**Error log**:
```
E1128 05:17:49.814731 Failed to get hf tokenizer for precise-prefix-cache-scorer
  mkdir /go: permission denied
```

**Root cause**: The EPP container runs as non-root user and the default
HuggingFace cache directory (/go/pkg/mod/.../bin/) is read-only.

**Fix**: Configure `tokenizersCacheDir: "/tmp/tokenizers"` in the
pluginsCustomConfig to use a writable directory.

Resolve Grafana deployment failure and enable automatic dashboard loading (#557)

* fix(monitoring): correct Prometheus and Grafana service names in documentation

The service names in the documentation did not match the actual services
created by the Helm chart. The install script uses RELEASE_NAME="llmd"
which creates services prefixed with 'llmd-', but the docs incorrectly
referenced 'prometheus-' prefixed services that don't exist.

This would cause 'service not found' errors when users tried to follow
the documented port-forward commands.

Changed:
- prometheus-kube-prometheus-prometheus → llmd-kube-prometheus-stack-prometheus
- prometheus-grafana → llmd-grafana

Signed-off-by: Pete Cheslock <pete.cheslock@redhat.com>

* feat(monitoring): enable Grafana sidecar for automatic dashboard discovery

The kube-prometheus-stack Helm chart includes a Grafana sidecar that can
automatically discover and load dashboards from Kubernetes ConfigMaps,
but this feature was not enabled in the installation script.

Without the sidecar enabled, users had to manually import dashboard JSON
files via the Grafana UI, which is cumbersome and error-prone.

This change enables the sidecar with:
- Dashboard discovery via ConfigMaps labeled with 'grafana_dashboard=1'
- Folder organization via 'grafana_folder' annotation
- Central mode: searches ALL namespaces
- Individual mode: searches only the monitoring namespace

Dashboards will now be automatically provisioned within 30 seconds of
ConfigMap creation.

Signed-off-by: Pete Cheslock <pete.cheslock@redhat.com>

* feat(monitoring): automatically load llm-d dashboards during installation

Add automatic dashboard loading during Prometheus/Grafana installation
to provide users with working dashboards out of the box.

Changes:
- Created load-llm-d-dashboards.sh script that reads all dashboard JSON
  files from docs/monitoring/grafana/dashboards/ and creates ConfigMaps
  with the appropriate labels for Grafana sidecar discovery
- Modified install-prometheus-grafana.sh to automatically call the
  dashboard loader after Prometheus installation
- Dashboards are loaded into ConfigMaps in the monitoring namespace

The dashboard loader creates ConfigMaps with:
- Label: grafana_dashboard=1 (for sidecar discovery)
- Naming pattern: llmd-<dashboard-name>
- Automatic conflict resolution via kubectl apply

This eliminates the need for users to manually import dashboard JSON
files and ensures a consistent dashboard experience across deployments.

Signed-off-by: Pete Cheslock <pete.cheslock@redhat.com>

* feat(monitoring): add llm-d Performance dashboard

Add a comprehensive inference performance dashboard optimized for
monitoring vLLM deployments

Dashboard features:
- Time to First Token (TTFT) latency percentiles (P50/P95/P99)
- Inter-token latency metrics
- KV cache hit rates (overall and per-pod)
- CPU cache usage monitoring
- Request throughput and queue status
- EPP pool health and load metrics
- EPP KV cache pool utilization

Key characteristics:
- Port-agnostic queries (filters by namespace and model, not port)
- Works with any vLLM deployment (CPU or GPU)
- Variables for datasource, model, and namespace selection

This dashboard will be automatically loaded by the installation script
along with other llm-d dashboards.

Signed-off-by: Pete Cheslock <pete.cheslock@redhat.com>

* fix(monitoring): resolve Grafana crash from duplicate datasource configurations

The Grafana pod was crashing with "Only one datasource per organization can
be marked as default" error due to conflicting datasource configurations.

The kube-prometheus-stack Helm chart v80+ automatically creates a default
Prometheus datasource via the sidecar, even when custom datasources are
defined. This resulted in two datasources both marked as isDefault: true,
causing Grafana to fail during provisioning.

This change disables the chart's automatic datasource creation while
preserving the custom datasource configuration needed for:
- Correct service URLs with the llmd release name prefix
- Dynamic TLS configuration support (--enable-tls flag)
- Proper service discovery URLs

Changes made:
- Added `sidecar.datasources.defaultDatasourceEnabled: false`
- Applied to both central and individual monitoring modes
- Corrected service names in prometheus-grafana-stack.md documentation

This fix ensures Grafana starts successfully with only the custom datasource
configuration, avoiding conflicts with the chart's default behavior introduced

* fix(monitoring): correct metric label in llm-d Performance dashboard for vanilla Kubernetes

The dashboard was using kubernetes_namespace label in metric queries, which
doesn't exist in vanilla Kubernetes Prometheus deployments. This caused all
namespace-filtered queries to return no data.

The source dashboard was designed for Red Hat AI on OpenShift (rhaoi3-llm-d),
where the OpenShift monitoring stack includes custom relabeling rules that
rename the standard namespace label to kubernetes_namespace to avoid conflicts
with Prometheus's internal namespace label.

In vanilla Kubernetes (KIND, kubeadm, etc.), the Prometheus Operator's
PodMonitor and ServiceMonitor resources add metrics with the standard
namespace label without any renaming.

Changes made:
- Replaced all instances of kubernetes_namespace with namespace (18 occurrences)
- Affects all vLLM metric queries: TTFT, inter-token latency, KV cache metrics,
  prefix cache hit rates, and request throughput

This fix ensures the dashboard works correctly in vanilla Kubernetes
deployments while maintaining compatibility with the original dashboard
design for OpenShift environments (where the label would need to remain
kubernetes_namespace).

fix: increase startup probe and pod wait timeouts for IS nightly E2E (#852)

The nightly-e2e-inference-scheduling-ocp workflow (run #37) failed
because 4 of 8 Qwen3-32B decode pods did not become ready within
the 30m pod_wait_timeout. Root cause: 8 pods concurrently downloading
a ~60GB model from HuggingFace into ephemeral emptyDir volumes caused
network contention. One pod on node pokprod-b93r38s1 was killed by
the startup probe (failureThreshold=60 x periodSeconds=30 = 30min)
and restarted, making it impossible to finish within the wait window.

Changes:
- Increase startupProbe failureThreshold from 60 to 120 (30min → 60min)
  to tolerate slow cold-cache model downloads under contention
- Increase pod_wait_timeout from 30m to 60m to match
- Correct required_gpus from 2 to 16 (8 replicas x 2 GPUs each)
  and recommended_gpus from 4 to 16 so the GPU availability check
  reflects actual demand

Route all tracing through an OTel Collector instead of exporting directly
to Jaeger. The new install script deploys both the collector and Jaeger
into the user-specified namespace (-n required). It auto-detects the
OpenTelemetry Operator CRD and uses an OpenTelemetryCollector CR when
available, falling back to a standalone Deployment otherwise. Both paths
produce the same service name (otel-collector) so all chart defaults use
the short name http://otel-collector:4317, resolving within the workload
namespace with no cross-namespace references.

ci: use pull_request for upstream PRs, pull_request_target for forks (#1023)

Previously all PRs used pull_request_target, which always runs the
workflow YAML from the base branch (main). This meant upstream PRs
that modify workflow files (build args, new jobs, etc.) wouldn't see
their changes take effect until merged.

Now:
- pull_request fires for upstream PRs (head repo == base repo),
  running the PR branch's workflow code. Org members' workflow
  changes take effect immediately in CI.
- pull_request_target fires only for fork PRs with 'ok-to-build'
  label, running main's workflow code safely.
- The fork-gate job ensures only one trigger proceeds per PR to
  avoid duplicate runs.

Signed-off-by: greg pereira <grpereir@redhat.com>

fix(docker): add LIBRARY_PATH and ldconfig to CUDA runtime stage (#1147)

The runtime stage of Dockerfile.cuda sets LD_LIBRARY_PATH (for the
runtime dynamic linker) but not LIBRARY_PATH (for the compile-time
linker invoked by gcc). When torch inductor JIT-compiles CUDA utilities
via gcc -l:libcuda.so.1, the compile-time linker cannot find
libcuda.so.1 because it is not in any of its search paths. This causes
vLLM to crash on GKE and other environments where the NVIDIA driver is
mounted at runtime into /usr/local/nvidia/lib64/.

Add LIBRARY_PATH to the runtime ENV block  this is the primary fix,
exposing NVIDIA runtime-injected paths to the compile-time linker.
Paths mirror those already in LD_LIBRARY_PATH.

Also add ld.so.conf.d entries and ldconfig after library copies from
the builder stage. This rebuilds the dynamic linker cache for gdrcopy,
UCX, NVSHMEM, and NIXL libraries, reducing reliance on LD_LIBRARY_PATH
alone for runtime resolution. Pattern matches Dockerfile.rdma-tools
runtime stage and the builder stage of this file.

Fixes #1063

* docs: add well-lit paths documentation

Add user-facing documentation for all 5 well-lit paths covering when
to use each path, key decisions, progressive tuning, observability,
and troubleshooting. Deployment steps link to the corresponding
guides rather than inlining commands.

Adopts the guides README language and framing. All terminology
validated against guide READMEs.

* docs: fix incorrect claim that scheduling modes compose

The precise prefix cache scorer and predicted latency scorer are
mutually exclusive replacements for the default prefix cache scorer,
not additive modes that can be stacked.

* docs: address PR review comments on well-lit paths

- Remove blog links paragraph from scheduling overview
- Fix Precise Prefix Cache "when to use" to reflect actual use cases
  (multi-modal, hybrid-model, near saturation regime)
- Remove incorrect claim that scheduling modes compose
- Rename "Default Scheduling" to "Load-Aware and Approximate Prefix
  Cache Scheduling"

* docs: restructure well-lit paths to match deck and add architecture diagrams

Flatten page structure to 5 top-level paths matching the deck:
Intelligent Inference Scheduling, P/D Disaggregation, KV Cache Management,
Wide Expert Parallelism, and Flow Control. Add SVG architecture diagrams
for each path using llm-d purple color scheme. Incorporate README intro
from PR #1179. Archive previous pages that are not yet in the deck.

precise-prefix-cache-scheduling guide helm -> kustomize (#1258)

* Refactor precise-prefix-cache-aware guide: helmfile -> kustomize, PR #862 config

Mirror the kustomize structure introduced by #1131 (inference-scheduling ->
optimized-baseline) and adopt the data-layer config shape from
llm-d/llm-d-inference-scheduler#862 (EndpointExtractor via endpoint-notification-source).

Central ZMQ stays the default (single scheduler replica, vLLM PUBs connect
into the EPP service). Pod discovery moves to a layered overlay plus a
kustomize component, documented as a sub-guide for active-active deployments.
Seven accelerator overlays for parity with optimized-baseline. UDS tokenizer
sidecar remains the default, paired with the `tokenizer` plugin on the UDS
socket so the EPP main container stays tokenizer-free.

Port in vLLM --kv-events-config is a POD_PORT env var (default "8000") so the
topic and --port can't drift.

Signed-off-by: Maroon Ayoub <maroon.ayoub@ibm.com>

* Align guide with optimized-baseline layout + verified active-active HA

Directory renames (mirror liu-cong/llm-d optimized-baseline/): nvidia-gpu/ -> gpu/,
amd-gpu/ -> amd/. Default README rewritten in self-contained style (inline
prereq/install/verify/benchmark/cleanup, `kubectl apply -k`, port-forward 8000:8081).
Benchmark template picks up the ${PORT} substitution. SGLang mention removed
(scorer does support it).

Sub-guide renamed pod-discovery -> active-active (feature name was jargon;
the topology users care about is active-active HA). The component and values
file rename alongside. Sub-guide rewritten to cover the full topology
(ASCII diagram, verification steps, tradeoffs).

Chart constraints resolved with two workarounds:

1. UDS tokenizer sidecar via helm post-renderer. The standalone chart's
   `sidecar.*` slot is owned by its Envoy proxy -- overriding it would lose
   HTTP. New `scheduler/patches/uds-tokenizer/` dir is a helm v4
   postrenderer/v1 plugin (installable via `helm plugin install`) that
   appends a third container (`tokenizer-uds`) + two emptyDir volumes + a
   /tmp/tokenizer mount on the `epp` container. Same script also works as
   a helm v3 path-based --post-renderer. Both paths documented.

2. True active-active via `--ha-enable-leader-election=false`. The chart
   auto-adds `--ha-enable-leader-election` whenever replicas > 1, collapsing
   the deployment to active-passive (leader-only readiness). The chart also
   renders values.yaml `flags` as two separate args (`--key` then `"value"`)
   which pflag doesn't parse as `--key=value` for booleans. Workaround:
   embed `=false` into the key itself (`"ha-enable-leader-election=false": ""`)
   so the rendered `--key=false` single-arg form lands after the chart's bare
   flag and wins via pflag last-occurrence.

Other fixes from cluster testing:
- scheduler values: dropped embedded sidecar/volumes/volumeMounts (moved to
  the post-renderer), re-added `http:8081` to extraServicePorts (helm arrays
  replace on merge; chart default was being overwritten by my zmq:5556 entry).
- vLLM patches: POD_PORT env var (paired with POD_IP) parameterizes the
  kv-events topic port and --port flag so they can't drift.
- ZMQ port 5557 -> 5556 (5557 collided with an internal service).

Verified live on an IBM OpenShift cluster with Qwen/Qwen3-32B across 2
vLLM replicas x TP=2:
- Central mode: repeat prompt landed `scores: {"<pod-ip>:8000": 2}` on the
  cache-warm pod from the EPP index populated via ZMQ KV events.
- Active-active: both EPP replicas passed readiness (no leader-election
  collapse), each replica independently opened subscribers to each vLLM pod
  via the data-layer `endpoint-notification-source` -> scorer
  `ExtractEndpoint` path (llm-d-inference-scheduler#862), repeat prompts
  correctly returned non-empty indexed scores.

ci: migrate e2e-prefix-cache-xpu from helmfile to kustomize (#1297)

* feat(precise-prefix): per-accelerator XPU scheduler plugins override

The precise-prefix-cache-scorer recomputes vLLM's block hashes in EPP, so
its tokenizer.modelName, tokenizersPoolConfig.modelName, and blockSize must
match the model the vLLM overlay deploys. The shared scheduler values file
(scheduler/precise-prefix-cache-aware.values.yaml) inlines the nvidia-gpu
default (Qwen/Qwen3-32B, blockSize 64), so any accelerator that deploys a
different model silently drops prefix-cache scores to 0.

Add scheduler/plugins/xpu.yaml that re-ships the full plugins YAML with
Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B (matching modelserver/xpu/vllm/) and the same scoring
lineup (tokenizer + decode-filter + precise-prefix-cache-scorer +
kv-cache-utilization-scorer + queue-scorer + max-score-picker,
speculativeIndexing enabled, zmqEndpoint tcp://*:5556, blockSize 64).

Pair 1:1 with modelserver/xpu/vllm/. Loaded on the helm command via
--set-file 'inferenceExtension.pluginsCustomConfig.precise-prefix-cache-aware-plugins\.yaml'=...
(documented in the README in a follow-up commit).

The shared values file and all six other accelerators are unchanged, so
existing nvidia-gpu / OCP / CKS / GKE nightlies continue to work.

ci: install kustomize in client-setup install-deps.sh (#1319)

The precise-prefix-cache-aware guide's helm install passes
`--post-renderer ./scheduler/patches/uds-tokenizer/post-renderer.sh`,
and that script shells out to the standalone `kustomize` binary at
post-renderer.sh:14 (`kustomize build "$TMP"`). `kubectl kustomize`
is not a substitute because helm invokes the post-renderer as a
subprocess which calls the `kustomize` command directly.

install-deps.sh already covers git, curl, tar, yq, kubectl, helm,
helm-diff, and helmfile — kustomize was missing. Runners that rely
on install-deps.sh for their toolchain (e.g. the self-hosted xpu
runner on dut5043 that's currently running the nightly e2e-prefix-
cache-xpu workflow) hit `kustomize: command not found` on helm install,
causing the scheduler release to fail silently (`... | tee` swallows
the non-zero exit) and the rest of the job to cascade.

Symptom on the 2026-04-30 nightly on main:
  https://github.com/llm-d/llm-d/actions/runs/25162029331
  Error: INSTALLATION FAILED: error while running post render on files:
    error while running command .../post-renderer.sh. error output:
    .../post-renderer.sh: line 14: kustomize: command not found

Add kustomize to the install-deps.sh list, following the existing
install_from_tarball pattern. Pinned to v5.7.1 (matches the client-
setup README's "v5.0.0+" baseline).

The fix is also latent-bug-preventive for e2e-optimized-baseline-xpu:
its lines 137 (`kustomize edit set image`) and 236 (`kustomize build |
kubectl delete -f -`) would hit the same missing-binary on a fresh
runner. Those paths currently only run when custom_image_tag is set
or during cleanup where errors are swallowed, so the bug hasn't
surfaced there yet.

Signed-off-by: Robin Zhang <zhangxiaojunhust@gmail.com>

ci: migrate e2e-pd-xpu from helmfile to kustomize (#1304)

PR #1238 migrated the pd-disaggregation guide from helmfile to kustomize,
removing the helmfile, helm-value envs (xpu), the ms-pd/infra-pd/gaie-pd
values layout and the httproute.yaml file that the old XPU workflow
depended on. The current .github/workflows/e2e-pd-xpu.yaml is still
wired for the pre-migration shape (helmfile apply -e xpu, httproute.yaml
sed patch, helmfile destroy) and would fail as soon as #1238 lands.

Rewrite it to match the kustomize + helm-standalone pattern now used by
the other well-lit paths:

- helm install pd-disaggregation oci://.../standalone
    -f guides/recipes/scheduler/base.values.yaml
    -f guides/pd-disaggregation/scheduler/pd-disaggregation.values.yaml
    --version v1.4.0
  No --post-renderer and no --set-file — unlike precise-prefix, the PD
  scheduler values have no embedded modelName coupling per accelerator.
- kubectl apply -k guides/pd-disaggregation/modelserver/xpu/vllm
  with `kustomize edit set image REPLACE_MODEL_SERVER_IMAGE=...` to
  override both decode and prefill deployments via the shared
  placeholder when `custom_image_tag` is provided.
- GATEWAY_HOST=pd-disaggregation-epp.<ns>.svc.cluster.local for
  e2e-validate.sh (standalone mode, no Gateway/HTTPRoute).
- Role-labelled (decode / prefill) log buckets on artifact upload for
  easier PD post-mortems.
- Pod wait timeout bumped 10m -> 15m to accommodate 4 XPU pods
  cold-starting and the NIXL side-channel handshake on BMG.
- Cron offset to 10:30 UTC (optimized-baseline-xpu is 10:00 UTC) to
  avoid back-to-back spikes on the self-hosted runner.

Mirrors the structural pattern established by
`e2e-optimized-baseline-xpu.yaml` (PR #1251) and
`e2e-prefix-cache-xpu.yaml` (PR #1297), and uses the same helm+kustomize
deploy pair as the merged `nightly-e2e-pd-disaggregation-cks.yaml`.

Verified locally on bmg817225 (8x Intel Arc Pro B60 / xe, kind cluster
with DRA). Scheduler EPP 2/2, decode 2/2, prefill 1/1 Ready in ~2m44s;
`/v1/completions` returned a correct Qwen3-0.6B response; EPP logs show
the disagg-profile-handler pipeline routed the request and the decode
pod logged a successful NIXL compatibility check (KV-transfer handshake
with prefill).

fix: use WORKFLOW_TOKEN for fork PR /test-nightly push (#1335)

* fix: use WORKFLOW_TOKEN for fork PR temp branch push

The default GITHUB_TOKEN cannot push branches containing workflow files
(.github/workflows/) — GitHub blocks this with: 'refusing to allow a
GitHub App to create or update workflow without workflows permission'.

The workflows scope can only be granted to PATs or GitHub App tokens,
not the built-in GITHUB_TOKEN. Switch to a dedicated WORKFLOW_TOKEN
secret that has contents:write + workflows permissions.

Prerequisite: create a WORKFLOW_TOKEN repo/org secret with a PAT (or
GitHub App token) that has the 'workflows' scope enabled.

Signed-off-by: Andrew Anderson <andy@clubanderson.com>

* fix: restore workflows:write permission removed in #1260

PR #1260 (Apr 24) removed 'workflows: write' from the permissions
block. This broke /test-nightly for fork PRs because pushing a temp
branch containing .github/workflows/ files requires that permission.

The permission was originally added in PR #1245 (Apr 23) for exactly
this reason. Restoring it — no separate PAT needed since the org
settings allow workflows scope on GITHUB_TOKEN.

Fix/predicted latency duplicate metrics port (#1406)

* [CI] Fix empty payload in predicted-latency e2e warmup

`kubectl exec ... -- sh -c "cat > /tmp/payload.json" <<<"$PAYLOAD"`
silently produces a 0-byte file: cat's stdin never receives the data
through `sh -c`, even when -i is passed. The warmup curls then sent
empty request bodies, vLLM rejected all of them, and the script aborted
at "zero successful warmup requests — gateway/model server is not
serving traffic" with ok=0 fail=100, even though the smoke loop just
before had succeeded against the same gateway.

Pipe through `tee` instead — when the inner command is the direct stdin
consumer (rather than a redirect inside `sh -c`), `kubectl exec -i`
delivers stdin reliably.

Reproduced on a live cluster:
  sh -c 'cat > file' → 0 bytes
  tee /tmp/file       → 76 bytes (correct)

This unblocks Run #3 of nightly-e2e-predicted-latency-gke (the deploy
step now passes after the duplicate-port fix; the validate step was
the next failure).

Signed-off-by: kaushikmitr <kaushikmitra.umd@gmail.com>

* [CI] Disable EPP metrics auth for predicted-latency nightlies

The chart defaults to --metrics-endpoint-auth=true, which 401s requests
without a service-account bearer token. e2e-validate-predicted-latency.sh
runs in a generic curlimages/curl pod with no token, so /metrics scrapes
return 401 → empty body → sum_histogram_count returns 0 →
"predicted TTFT histogram is empty after 100 requests."

Pass --set inferenceExtension.monitoring.prometheus.auth.enabled=false
to the chart's helm install for all three nightlies (GKE/CKS/OCP).
This adds --metrics-endpoint-auth=false to the EPP container args. Only
affects CI; the production guide default (auth on) is unchanged.

Verified locally: predicted_ttft_count goes from 0 → matches request
count, and the validate script reports "Predicted-latency scheduling
is active."

optimized-baseline: mount /.triton and /.config emptyDirs for non-root pods (#1450)

* optimized-baseline: mount /.triton and /.config emptyDirs for non-root pods

The vllm/vllm-openai image's engine init writes to /.triton (Triton
compiler cache, fatal) and /.config (vllm usage_lib, non-fatal but
log-noisy) at filesystem root. On clusters that enforce non-root
execution by default — OpenShift's restricted-v2 SCC, or plain k8s
under PSA restricted with a non-root pod security policy — both writes
fail with PermissionError.

The existing /.cache + torch-compile-cache mount is precedent: same
shape, same intent. The nightly OpenShift CI in
.github/workflows/nightly-e2e-optimized-baseline-ocp.yaml already
patches /.triton in at runtime via yq; baking it into the base
manifest removes the patch and makes the documented quickstart work
on OpenShift out of the box.

Verified end-to-end against an OpenShift 4.x cluster with default
restricted-v2 SCC, vllm/vllm-openai:v0.19.1, and a real workload
(Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507 on 2x L40S, TP=2): the unpatched manifest
CrashLoopBackOffs with the exact PermissionError stack trace from
the issue body; the patched manifest boots cleanly past Triton kernel
compilation and serves chat completions.

Closes #1430.

* Add nightly E2E caller workflows for XPU guides

Three thin callers that delegate to the new reusable workflow
reusable-nightly-e2e-xpu-helmfile.yaml in llm-d/llm-d-infra, mirroring
the nightly-e2e-*-gke.yaml pattern from PR #747:

- nightly-e2e-inference-scheduling-xpu.yaml (10:00 UTC)
- nightly-e2e-pd-disaggregation-xpu.yaml    (10:30 UTC)
- nightly-e2e-prefix-cache-xpu.yaml         (11:00 UTC)

Staggered to avoid contention on the single-host xpu runner (the three
existing e2e-*-xpu.yaml workflows all fire at 10:00 UTC and queue
serially). The existing workflows are left in place; cleanup of their
cron triggers will follow in a separate PR, matching the GKE migration
approach (PR #747 added callers, PR #1226 removed old crons).

Each caller passes the guide's default RELEASE_NAME_POSTFIX, so the
nightly deploys the same resource names a user running the guide
per its README would. The reusable applies the checked-in
guides/<guide>/httproute.yaml as-is — no xpu-specific httproute files
are introduced.

Blocked on: llm-d/llm-d-infra PR adding
reusable-nightly-e2e-xpu-helmfile.yaml. Until that merges the
`uses:` reference will not resolve and these workflows cannot run.

via `helm install` of the GAIE standalone chart + `kubectl apply -k` on
guides/<guide>/modelserver/xpu/vllm/, not helmfile. That changed the
file basename (dropped `-helmfile`) and the input contract (removed
`release_name_postfix` and `httproute_file`, added
`scheduler_release_name`, `scheduler_values_files`, `helm_post_renderer`,
etc.). Also, `inference-scheduling` was renamed to `optimized-baseline`
upstream.

  * nightly-e2e-pd-disaggregation-xpu.yaml    (10:30 UTC)
  * nightly-e2e-precise-prefix-cache-xpu.yaml (11:00 UTC)

Each supplies its guide's canonical `scheduler_values_files` stack as
documented in the guide README. The precise-prefix caller passes the
UDS-tokenizer post-renderer script directly (helm v3 accepts a path;
install-deps.sh pins v3.19.0) so no helm plugin install is needed.

avoids contention on the single-host xpu runner.

fix(ci): decouple router chart version from GAIE_VERSION in XPU/HPU e2e workflows (#1639)

The 4 XPU/HPU e2e workflows reuse GAIE_VERSION (v1.5.0) for both the
Gateway API Inference Extension CRD installation and the helm install
--version flag for llm-d-router-standalone-dev. These are different
artifacts with independent versioning: GAIE CRDs follow upstream
kubernetes-sigs/gateway-api-inference-extension tags, while the router
chart uses its own semver (currently v0 series).

Passing GAIE_VERSION=v1.5.0 as the chart version causes helm to look
for a non-existent chart version, failing the 'Deploy scheduler via
helm' step in all 4 workflows.

Add ROUTER_CHART_VERSION=v0 to each job's env block and use it for
helm install --version, matching the pattern already used by all
nightly e2e workflows. GAIE_VERSION remains for CRD installation.

Affected workflows:
- e2e-optimized-baseline-xpu.yaml
- e2e-pd-xpu.yaml
- e2e-prefix-cache-xpu.yaml
- e2e-optimized-baseline-hpu.yaml

chore(guides): add OWNERS files to all well-lit path guides (#1663)

Adds an OWNERS file to each guide with approvers, reviewers, and auto-assign fields enabled, keeping the reviewers list synchronized with the approvers.

Below is a summary of each guide and their designated owners:

1. Asynchronous Processing (asynchronous-processing)
   Summary: Process inference requests asynchronously using a queue-based architecture for batch workloads.
   Owners: @shimib

2. Batch Gateway (batch-gateway)
   Summary: Submit, track, and manage large-scale batch inference jobs via an OpenAI-compatible Batch API.
   Owners: @lioraron

3. Flow Control (flow-control)
   Summary: Intelligent request queuing for multi-tenant deployments and managing traffic spikes.
   Owners: @LukeAVanDrie

4. No-Kubernetes Deployment (no-kubernetes-deployment)
   Summary: Standard deployment guide for running llm-d on bare metal or standard VM-based environments.
   Owners: @ezrasilvera

5. Optimized Baseline (optimized-baseline)
   Summary: Deploy vLLM with prefix-cache and load-aware routing enabled by the llm-d EPP.
   Owners: @liu-cong, @vMaroon

6. Prefill/Decode Disaggregation (pd-disaggregation)
   Summary: Split inference into specialized prefill and decode instances to improve throughput and QoS.
   Owners: @tlrmchlsmth

7. Precise Prefix Cache Routing (precise-prefix-cache-routing)
   Summary: Enhance optimized baseline with precise global indexing of the vLLM KV cache state.
   Owners: @vMaroon, @liu-cong

8. Predicted Latency-Based Routing (predicted-latency-routing)
   Summary: Enhance optimized baseline with real-time predictions of request latency via an XGBoost model.
   Owners: @kaushikmitr

9. Recipes (recipes)
   Summary: Reusable components and overlays for deployment configurations (gateway, modelserver, router).
   Owners: @ahg-g, @robertgshaw2-redhat, @liu-cong, @Gregory-Pereira

10. Rollouts (rollouts)
    Summary: Perform incremental rollout operations for LoRA adapters, base models, and model server versions.
    Owners: @ahg-g

11. Tiered Prefix Cache (tiered-prefix-cache)
    Summary: Offload KV caches beyond accelerator memory to CPU or disk to increase working set size.
    Owners: @kfirtoledo, @liu-cong, @vMaroon

12. Wide Expert-Parallelism (wide-ep-lws)
    Summary: Deploy large Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models over multiple nodes via DP/EP configurations.
    Owners: @robertgshaw2-redhat, @tlrmchlsmth

13. Workload Autoscaling (workload-autoscaling)
    Summary: Autoscale the LLM service via proactive, SLO-aware signals reflecting true state of the inference system.
    Owners: @lionelvillard

Normalize the names of "nightly E2E" workflows (#1721)

This PRs does not introduce any changes into the workflows, it merely renames
these files in a normalized manner.

The normalized names follow the convention:

`<workflow>-<guide>-<provider>-<offload destination>-<accelerator>-<inference
engine>-<cache connector>.yaml`

Where:
`<guide>` is the list provided by `$(find guides/ -maxdepth 2 -name README.md
-print | grep -Ev "rollouts|prereqs|recipes|guides/README.md")`
`<provider>` indicates which companies/members (and teams) are providing
hardware resources for testing (currently, `cks`, `gke`, `ibm`, `intel` and
`amd`)
`<offload destination>` possible values are `acc` (indicating that no offloading
is done, as all blocks are retined within the accelerator), `gpu`, `storage`
`<accelerator>`: `gpu`, `tpu`, `rocm`, `xpu` and `hpu`
`<cache connector>`: `x` (for "don't care"/"not defined"), `native` (for `vllm`)
and `lmcache`

fix(gke): override RDMA resource requests to fix scheduling on H200 (#1738)

* fix(gke): override RDMA resource requests to fix scheduling on H200

GKE Warden mutating webhook automatically injects resource requests for both
networking.gke.io.networks/rdma-X and networking.gke.io.networks/rdma-X.IP.
However, modern GKE H200 (A3 Ultra) nodes only advertise the .IP variant, which
prevents pods from scheduling.

Explicitly setting the legacy networking.gke.io.networks/rdma-X limits to 0
prevents the webhook from injecting the resource requests for the non-.IP variant.
This resolves the scheduling deadlock on H200 nodes while maintaining compatibility,
since the webhook still injects the .IP variant.

ci: add nightly e2e for the flow-control guide (#1728)

* ci: add flow-control e2e validation script

The default e2e smoke test sends single sequential requests, but flow
control is work-conserving, so those never queue and never exercise the
feature. This validator forces contention across the three priority
bands and checks the guarantees that matter: per-band queue isolation
and priority-ordered (QoS) dispatch.

Assertions rest on cumulative histogram metrics (queue_duration count
and mean wait), which are insensitive to scrape timing; the queue_size
and pool_saturation gauges are logged for context only.

Refs #1360

Signed-off-by: Luke Van Drie <lukevandrie@google.com>

* ci: add flow-control nightly e2e workflow

Wires the flow-control guide into the nightly GKE e2e lane: reuses the
optimized-baseline model servers (relabeled) and the standalone router
chart with the flowControl gate, then dispatches to
e2e-validate-flow-control.sh via --extra-validate.

To make backpressure deterministic on a small CI pool, the deploy lowers
the concurrency-detector maxConcurrency by key -- not by its current
value, so a future retune cannot silently no-op it -- and fails if the
override does not take.

GPU is used only because every live e2e lane targets the GPU/cloud
reusable workflows; flow control itself is accelerator-agnostic.

Refs #1360

optimized-baseline: mount /.triton and /.config emptyDirs on non-gpu vllm variants (#1711)

The vllm/vllm-openai engine writes a Triton compiler cache to /.triton (fatal) and a usage_lib config to /.config (non-fatal) at the filesystem root, since HOME=/ for non-root containers. On clusters that enforce non-root execution (OpenShift restricted-v2 SCC, or k8s under PSA restricted), both writes fail with PermissionError and the /.triton failure crashes the model server, as reported in #1311.

PR #1450 baked these emptyDir mounts into the gpu variant. The remaining vllm variants of this guide were not updated and still hit the crash under a restricted SecurityContext. This applies the same mounts to amd, cpu, tpu-v6, tpu-v7 and xpu, matching the gpu variant and the precise-prefix-cache-routing guide (which already mounts /.triton on all of its variants). hpu already sets DO_NOT_TRACK=1, so it does not write /.config and only needed the /.triton mount.

Verified with kustomize build and kubectl apply --dry-run on each variant: the rendered Deployments carry the triton-cache and vllm-config volumes.

Closes #1311

* fix: remove duplicate hardcoded images from CPU patches

The cpu-vllm Kustomize Component already defines
ghcr.io/llm-d/llm-d-cpu:v0.6.0 via the images transformer (matching
REPLACE_MODEL_SERVER_IMAGE from the base). Having the same image

component from controlling the image: patches run before the images
transformer, so the placeholder is gone by the time the transformer

plus the clean per-version-aware paths means the buttons stay in the
current /docs/<version>/ context instead of doing hard navigations that
cross version boundaries (which would 404 against routes that don't exist
in the current Docusaurus app).

landing for the website). The website-side sync-docs.sh prefers .mdx
when it exists.

- "Get started" CTA: `<Link to="/getting-started/quickstart">` instead of
  `<a href="./quickstart">`. The relative `./` form 404s with
  `trailingSlash: false`; the absolute Link form is SPA-routed and
  version-aware.
- "View performance analysis" CTA: `<Link>` with `target="_blank"`
  pointing to https://prism.llm-d.ai/.

guides/precise-prefix-cache-routing: run the renderer as a Service, not an EPP sidecar (#1871)

* guides/precise-prefix-cache-routing: run the renderer as a Service, not an EPP sidecar

The tokenizer renderer was injected as a per-EPP-pod `vllm-render` sidecar by
the standalone chart (`router.tokenizer.enabled: true`). That couples render
capacity to the EPP replica count and duplicates the tokenizer in every EPP pod.

Replace it with a standalone, horizontally-scalable render Service:
- Add `render/` kustomize overlay: a `vllm launch render` Deployment (3 replicas)
  + ClusterIP Service, mirroring the chart's sidecar container spec.
- Disable the sidecar (`router.tokenizer.enabled: false`) and point the EPP
  `token-producer` plugin at the Service
  (`http://precise-prefix-cache-routing-render:8000`).
- Keep the `llm-d.ai/guide` label off render pods — it is the InferencePool /
  model-server selector, so labeled render pods would be treated as routable
  model servers (and the EPP would try to ZMQ-subscribe to their nonexistent
  :5556 KV-event socket).
- README: document deploying/cleaning up the render Service + the label caveat.
- CI: dry-run the new render overlay; correct the stale sidecar comments.

Pin the GPU vLLM model server and the renderer to vllm/vllm-openai{,-cpu}:v0.23.0.

Validated on 16xH100 (8x Qwen3-32B, TP=2) with EPP image
ghcr.io/llm-d/llm-d-router-endpoint-picker:v0.9.0-rc.2: the full
guide_precise-prefix-cache-routing_1.yaml ladder (rates 3->60) ran with 0
request failures; the 3 render pods served ~17k tokenization requests, evenly
load-balanced, with 0 pod restarts.

Signed-off-by: Maroon Ayoub <mayoub@redhat.com>

* precise-prefix-cache-routing/render: address review feedback

- Fix HF cache mount: point HF_HOME at the mounted emptyDir (/tmp/hf) so the
  cache volume actually backs the tokenizer files in use (was /tmp/hf/hub with
  the volume mounted at /root/.cache/huggingface).
- Add resource limits (cpu/memory == requests), matching the repo's vLLM
  manifests.
- Set DO_NOT_TRACK=1 to disable vLLM telemetry, consistent with the model
  server patch (avoids /.config writes under restricted SecurityContexts).
- Scope the render Service selector: add a guide-specific
  `app.kubernetes.io/part-of: precise-prefix-cache-routing` label (deliberately
  not `llm-d.ai/guide`, the InferencePool selector) to both the Deployment
  selector and the Service so a `vllm-render` pod from another guide in a shared
  namespace cannot be cross-selected.
- Drop unused API access (automountServiceAccountToken: false).

Signed-off-by: Maroon Ayoub <mayoub@redhat.com>

* precise-prefix-cache-routing/render: address review feedback (round 2)

- Right-size render resources for the 3-replica pool (per review): requests
  drop to cpu 1 / 4Gi (was 4 / 8Gi), limits raised to cpu 4 / 12Gi. Tokenization
  is light and bursty, so a small reservation with headroom fits better than
  reserving 4 cores per replica.
- Drop the redundant `includeSelectors:/includeTemplates: false` from the render
  kustomization `labels` block (those are the kustomize defaults); keep the
  comment explaining why the guide label stays off pods/selectors.
- Remove the explicit `router.tokenizer.enabled: false` override — the chart
  already defaults the tokenizer sidecar off. Update the surrounding
  comments/README/CI note to say so instead of referencing the removed key.

predicted-latency-routing: add the P/D disaggregated deployment and its benchmark (#2048)

Predicted-latency scheduling composes with prefill/decode disaggregation, but the
guide had no path for it. Add a third router values file that layers the latency
predictor onto the pd-disaggregation pipeline: prefill is picked purely on
predicted TTFT and decode purely on predicted TPOT, since each stage owns only
half of a request's latency, and the prefix-cache affinity filter runs on prefill
only (in P/D the cache lives on the prefill pods; decode receives KV over NIXL,
so decode-side affinity adds nothing and skews balance).

Document the deployment (reusing the pd-disaggregation model server unchanged),
the benchmark that drives it, and the results: gpt-oss-120b across 8 prefill TP1
+ 2 decode TP4 on 16x H200 with KV transfer over RDMA/RoCE. The baseline is the
router the pd-disaggregation guide ships today (prefix-cache + queue +
KV-utilization scorers on prefill, active-request scorer on decode). Both
saturate the same ceiling (44.3 req/s, ~234K tok/s) with identical throughput and
TPOT; the predictor's gain is in the TTFT tails as load rises -- at 45 req/s,
p50 -20%, p90 -25%, p99 -62%.

The P/D and SLO files set streamingMode: true, since both depend on predicted
TPOT (decode placement, and TPOT SLO enforcement) and TPOT is trained from the
inter-token gaps of a streamed response; clients must send "stream": true. The
routing-only file keeps training on end-to-end latency and needs no such change.

Also set ttftSource: latencyPredictor on the affinity filters in all three values
files so the filter's TTFT load-gate comes from the predictor rather than the
heuristic estimate, and point the GPU benchmark case at this guide's own
inference-perf workload template.

Switch the P/D scheduling profiles to token-based routing: the prefill
profile uses prefix-cache-affinity-filter + token-load-scorer (fed by the
approx prefix-cache and inflight-load producers), and the pure-decode
profile scores on active-request-scorer alone, since decode is bound by
concurrent in-flight requests rather than prefill throughput.

recipe through the full P/D path (NIXL transfer included) on the
reference fleet: gpt-oss-120b, 8x prefill TP=1 + 2x decode TP=4 on H200.
The EPP runs a single replica so in-flight token accounting stays whole.

In a same-fleet A/B against the previous weighted scorer profiles, the
token-based config delivered equal or higher output throughput at every
rung of a 10-45 QPS sweep (+5% at rate 45: 12,036 vs 11,426 tok/s) with
equal or better TTFT tails and zero failed requests on both arms.

Refresh the benchmarking report with the rate=45 stage from this config
measured on GKE A3 Ultra (H200, DRANet RoCE via DRA): 12,036 output

guides: add SLO-driven autoscaling (KEDA + predicted latency) (#2011)

* guides: add SLO-driven autoscaling (KEDA + predicted latency)

A guide to autoscale a vLLM inference pool against latency SLOs using only
off-the-shelf components: the EPP's predicted-latency histograms, a Prometheus
recording rule for the saturation signal, and a KEDA ScaledObject whose
expr-lang formula computes the desired replica count and drives a standard HPA.
No custom controller.

Includes the control-law math (signal chain, hysteresis, in-flight credit),
the deployable manifests (recording rules, ScaledObject, kube-state-metrics),
the EPP plugin config, and a reproducible benchmark harness with results
(95.8% combined SLO attainment at 5.93 avg replicas vs 100% at a static 8).

[ROCM] optimized-baseline: persist model cache for AMD vllm via component (#2153)

The AMD optimized-baseline overlay mounts HF_HOME on an emptyDir, so every
run re-downloads the model (Qwen/Qwen3-32B, ~65GB) from HuggingFace before
the benchmark starts. This is slow and, on bandwidth-constrained networks,
fragile (a stalled download can hang or fail the run).

Add a reusable "model-cache" component (guides/recipes/modelserver/components/
model-cache) that backs the cache with a persistent RWX PVC and points
HF_HOME at it, so the model downloads once and is reused across runs. The
volume is named generically (model-cache) so it is independent of the model
source; the PVC omits storageClassName so it binds the cluster's default
StorageClass (which must support ReadWriteMany).

Keep it cluster-specific and opt-in: the guide base is moved to base/ and
left as upstream (emptyDir), and a new amd-ci/ overlay layers the component
on top. Other guides can reuse the component from their own amd-ci/ overlay;
per-guide namespace isolation gives each its own PVC.

docs(async/multitenant): render prometheusURL, drop the MODEL_A/MODEL_B placeholders (#2145)

The render() helper did not cover everything the overlays need, and it
listed two placeholders that do not exist.

prometheusURL was hardcoded to the `monitoring` namespace in both
self-hosted-Prometheus overlays, with no placeholder and nothing in
render() to touch it. The guide's own Observability section installs
kube-prometheus-stack into `monitoring`, so the happy path works, but a
reader whose Prometheus lives anywhere else gets a URL that resolves to
nothing -- and it fails open, not closed: the Scenario C gates are
wait-on-refuse(prometheus-query) with "fallback":"1", and a budget of 1
is a wide-open gate. The demo then runs clean and demonstrates nothing.

Give prometheusURL a PROM_URL placeholder, render it, and default it in
render() to the URL that was hardcoded before, so an unset PROM_URL
reproduces today's behaviour exactly. Export PROM_URL in the guide's
environment block. saturation-gmp.yaml keeps its own URL: it points at
the GMP query frontend in NAMESPACE, which is already rendered.

Turn the silent case into a visible one. Scenario C now grep-checks the
rendered prometheusURL and, after the upgrade, runs three checks before
any conclusion is drawn from a run: the URL answers from inside the
cluster, the vLLM metric the gates read is actually present for POOL_A,
and the processor is not logging "using fallback value". Notes & gotchas
records that an unreachable Prometheus fails open.

MODEL_A/MODEL_B were listed under "Replace:" in all four overlays but
are not placeholders anywhere -- in the saturation overlays the only
occurrence is the Replace line itself, and in the quota-only overlays
they appear solely in prose explaining payload.model. Model names reach
the system through payload.model, which the guide's publish() helper
fills in from the shell. Drop them from the Replace lists, and say
plainly in the two quota-only headers and in the README that they are
the guide's shell variables, not overlay placeholders.

Verified by running the new render() over all four overlays: every
placeholder resolves, the YAML parses, prometheusURL comes out as the
overridden URL, and with PROM_URL unset it comes out byte-identical to
the previous hardcoded value.

Ref: https://github.com/llm-d/llm-d-async/issues/364

exercised by guides/asynchronous-processing/test/kind-e2e.sh and by

docs(guides): make the multitenant publish() helper burst (#2146)

The multitenant guide's scenarios call `publish batch a 100` and
`publish premium a 200 & publish batch a 200`, but publish() issued one
`kubectl exec` (Redis) or one `gcloud` invocation (Pub/Sub) per request.
At roughly a second apiece a single scenario spent minutes enqueuing, and
the workers drained the queue as fast as the loop filled it — so the
backlog Scenario B classifies as overflow, and the saturation Scenario C
needs, may never form. Three concurrent `publish ... &` calls also
interleaved their execs, setting arrival rates by exec latency rather
than by the requested counts.

Redis: build the score/member pairs first and send the batch in a single
`ZADD key score member score member ...`. Pub/Sub has no multi-message
publish, so cap PUBLISH_PAR (default 8) gcloud invocations in flight.

The batch now shares one score, so ZPopMin breaks ties on the member
string; zero-padding the index keeps that tie-break equal to publish
order. Message ids gain a per-call random token so two bursts to the same
queue in the same second cannot collide into a silent re-score. The batch
also shares one deadline, so PUBLISH_TTL (default 300, unchanged) can be
raised when a saturated pool will not drain in time.

Fixes llm-d/llm-d-async#366

docs(async/multitenant): make the saturation divisor a rendered SAT_CAP placeholder (#2135)

* docs(async/multitenant): make the saturation divisor a rendered SAT_CAP placeholder

Scenario C's saturation gate could never close with the guide's own worker-pool
sizes. The `prometheus-query` gate closes at budget <= 0, and `clamp(..., 0, 1)`
floors the budget at 0, so `clamp(1 - sum(vllm:num_requests_running{...})/20, 0, 1)`
only closes once 20 requests are running on that model. Each pool has 8 workers,
Scenario C's load is entirely async, and a worker evaluates the gate while holding
a message it has not dispatched yet -- so at most 7 of the pool's requests are ever
running at evaluation time. Nothing parked, and the run still completed and looked
healthy, so the named scenario silently never happened.

Replace the hardcoded `/20` with a `SAT_CAP` placeholder rendered by the guide's
existing sed `render()` helper (default `SAT_CAP=4` against `workers: 8`), and
state the sizing rule: SAT_CAP must stay below the pool's `workers`, or async load
alone can never close the gate. Scenario C now says what the reader should see --
model-a's budget hitting exactly 0 while model-b sits at ~1 -- and how to check
the parked pools via `llm_d_async_async_inflight_requests`. Also note in
Observability that `async_dispatch_budget` is the queue gates' budget; the pool
gate's budget is the PromQL expression itself.

Ref: https://github.com/llm-d/llm-d-async/issues/365
Signed-off-by: Shimi Bandiel <shimib@google.com>

* docs(async/multitenant): point saturation-gate observability at async_gate_metric_value

async_dispatch_budget is only written by the queue gates (redis
sortedset_impl / pubsubimpl), so it says nothing about the per-pool
saturation gates. Those are covered by async_gate_metric_value /
async_gate_metric_threshold, which MetricDispatchGate.Budget() writes on
every successful read, labelled by the owning pool_name. Because they are
written only on success, a missing or frozen value is itself the signal
that the gate has fallen back to its fallback budget.

Also give the SAT_CAP margin its second reason: the gate reads
vllm:num_requests_running through a 15s PodMonitor scrape plus
prometheusCacheTTL: 5s, so it acts on a count up to ~20s stale.

* Fix XPU image build by pinning a release base image and restoring oneAPI env

The XPU base image was pinned to vllm-ci-test-repo, a temporary registry whose
tags are garbage collected. The v0.23.0 tag has since been deleted, so every
XPU image build fails with "not found" before the Dockerfile even runs.

permanent. That image still ships oneAPI under /opt/intel/oneapi but no longer
exports its environment (vllm-project/vllm#45973), so icpx is off PATH and the
LMCache SYCL build cannot run. The guides launch the server with `bash -c`,
bypassing the entrypoint, so setvars.sh is never sourced at runtime either and
LMCache silently skips its xpu_ops backend rather than failing loudly.

Bake the variables setvars.sh would export into the image and set CPATH for the
build step. Verified locally: the image builds, torch.xpu sees all 16 devices,
and LMCache selects lmcache.xpu_ops without sourcing setvars.sh.

optimized-baseline EPP ConfigMap and merge-patch featureGates: [flowControl]

fix: Disable USE_SCCACHE when the sccache fallback kicks in (#2224)

* Disable USE_SCCACHE when the sccache fallback kicks in

When sccache cannot start, setup-sccache.sh removes the binary, unsets the
CMake launcher variables and returns success. It leaves USE_SCCACHE set to
true, and every consumer sources the script and then branches on that value,
so they still put sccache into CC/CXX or call sccache --show-stats.

gdrcopy builds with a plain Makefile, so clearing the CMAKE_* launchers does
nothing for it and the hardcoded sccache in CC is what breaks the build:

    make[1]: sccache: No such file or directory
    make[1]: *** [<builtin>: gdrapi.o] Error 127

This fails every CUDA-family image build. build-ucx.sh and build-nixl.sh set
CC the same way and would fail identically, and four scripts call bare
sccache --show-stats after the binary is gone, which aborts under set -e.

Export USE_SCCACHE=false in both fallback branches. The script is sourced, so
one change covers all consumers, matching what build-nvshmem.sh already does
when it opts out of sccache.

Verified by running build-gdrcopy.sh in a container with no sccache present:
it exits 2 with the error above before the change and 0 after.

Fixes #2223

Signed-off-by: yuanwu <yuan.wu@intel.com>

* Keep the sccache binary when the fallback disables caching

The degrade path deleted /usr/local/bin/sccache, but Dockerfile.cuda
copies it out of the builder stage into the final image. Now that
USE_SCCACHE is exported as false, every consumer of the binary is
already guarded, so there is nothing left to protect against.

Signed-off-by: yuanwu <yuan.wu@intel.com>

* Gate the sccache smoke test on USE_SCCACHE instead of the binary

install-sccache.sh used the presence of the binary as a proxy for
"setup-sccache succeeded", which only worked because the fallback
deleted it. Check the flag the fallback now clears.

Fix oneCCL init failure for tiered-prefix-cache on Intel XPU (#2270)

* Fix oneCCL init failure for tiered-prefix-cache on Intel XPU

The XPU decode pod crash-looped during standup with:
  oneCCL: atl_ofi_comm.cpp:232 init_transport: EXCEPTION: failed to initialize ATL
  CCL_ERROR| atl_ofi_helper.cpp:1118 fi_getinfo error: ret -61, providers 0

With tensor-parallel-size=4 the vLLM XPU worker initializes the xccl/oneCCL
backend, which defaults to the OFI transport. The bundled libfabric in the
container exposes no providers because FI_PROVIDER_PATH is unset, so ATL
initialization fails and the engine core never starts.

Point libfabric at the Intel MPI provider directory shipped in the image and
select the tcp provider. Verified on a kind cluster with Intel XPUs: the decode
pod now reaches Ready with tensor-parallel-size=4 and the OffloadingConnector.

Match llm-d.ai/model-id to the served model name (#2310)

WVA resolves a variant's model from this annotation and matches it against
the vLLM metric label model_name exactly. The guide serves Qwen/Qwen3-32B
with no --served-model-name, so its metrics carry the full repo id while
the annotation carries the short form. Every saturation query therefore
returns no series.

The failure is silent: WVA logs "No saturation metrics available for model,
skipping analysis" followed by "Optimization completed successfully", then
emits a desired replica count equal to the current one. KEDA consumes that
without falling back, so the ScaledObject reports Ready, Active and
Fallback=False while autoscaling never actually responds to load.

docs(router): drop monitoring values from the agentgateway install command (#2323)

PR #2138 removed features/monitoring.values.yaml from the canonical router
install commands because it renders a ServiceMonitor, which fails Helm
validation on any cluster without the Prometheus Operator CRDs. It covered the
Standalone with Envoy and Kubernetes Gateway API commands and missed the third
one, Standalone with agentgateway, which still carried the flag.

Nothing in the agentgateway path suppresses the ServiceMonitor:
agentgateway-proxy.values.yaml only overrides router.proxy.args, and
monitoring.values.yaml still sets router.monitoring.prometheus.enabled=true.
Rendering the documented command against the published chart emits
monitoring.coreos.com/v1 ServiceMonitor, so the install still aborts.

Also note that helm upgrade does not inherit the previous release's values. The
Enable Prometheus Monitoring section tells the reader to layer monitoring onto
an existing release, but its command carries neither agentgateway-proxy.values.yaml
nor the three --set flags, so an agentgateway user following it would revert
their proxy configuration to chart defaults.

The bespoke nightly deploy script hand-built the CRD manifest URLs as
releases/download/${VERSION}. GitHub uses a different path shape for
floating releases (releases/latest/download/<asset>) than for pinned
tags (releases/download/<tag>/<asset>), so once the post-release-cut
defaults resolved to "latest" the first kubectl apply 404ed and killed
the run (Nightly - Flow Control E2E (GKE GPU) #76).

guides/env.sh has computed GAIE_URL / ROUTER_RELEASE_URL for exactly
this since #2299, and the guide README already uses them; the script
(restored in #1918, which predates #2299) never picked them up. Switch
to the computed vars, matching the README prerequisites and
optimized-baseline's guide.yaml.

docs: drop the InternalRequest envelope from the Pub/Sub quickstart payload (#2328)

The Pub/Sub consumer unmarshals the message body into a bare
api.RequestMessage and builds the InternalRequest itself from the Pub/Sub
message ID and subscriber ID. Unlike the Redis path there is no
envelope-unwrapping step, so request_kind/internal/data are unknown fields;
encoding/json ignores them and the decode succeeds with every field zeroed,
including deadline, which makes the request instantly expired.

Publish the request on its own, matching the multitenant guide, and reword
the note above it to describe the Pub/Sub contract rather than the Redis one.

Fixes #2327

the lane on its schedule now that the workflows from #2469 are on main.

The ScaledObject in keda/base is named and labelled for the NVIDIA model
server, so an AMD kustomize component retargets it at the ROCm model server
and MI355X, and the wva guide points at the component.

The deploy script stands the stack up in the order the guide describes:
the optimized-baseline model server, then the EPP router, then the autoscaler
layer on top. It discovers the Prometheus namespace from the Prometheus CR and
picks the scheme from whether a web TLS secret exists, so it works against both
a TLS and a plain HTTP monitoring stack, and it fails fast with a clear message
if the expected Prometheus service is not there rather than timing out later.
It also layers the monitoring component onto the model server, since the
optimized-baseline model server bases ship no PodMonitor and the autoscaler has
no saturation input without one. ClusterRoleBindings carry a namespace hash and
a namespace label so the lane neither collides with nor outlives the four other
nightlies on the shared cluster.

The two workflows merged dispatch-only, so that main never referenced a deploy
script that was not there yet. With the script landing here, the 13:00 UTC
nightly and the 15:00 UTC status roll-up go back on their crons, clear of the
03:00, 05:00, 07:00 and 10:00 slots the other four ROCm nightlies hold.

Validated end to end on the ROCm CI cluster: the autoscaler made real scaling
decisions off live vLLM metrics, KEDA consumed the published desired replica
count, e2e-validate.sh passed 10/10, and teardown left no residue.

docs: add token-aware autoscaling guide (KEDA + EPP token backlog) (#2466)

* docs: add token-aware autoscaling guide (KEDA + EPP token backlog)

Adds guides/workload-autoscaling/keda-epp-token-aware, a KEDA + EPP
autoscaling path that scales on tokens of outstanding work rather than a
count of requests. An 8192-token prompt is 16x the prefill work of a
512-token one and a queue-depth or running-request counter rates them the
same, so the same request rate can mean a third of a replica or three
replicas of prefill work.

Two triggers, each measured in its own unit:

  * prefill divides the EPP's llm_d_epp_inflight_tokens backlog by a
    calibrated peakPrefillThroughput, turning tokens into SECONDS of queue
    wait — directly comparable to a share of a TTFT SLO, so the threshold
    is derivable (threshold ~= TTFT_SLO - ISL/V_P) rather than tuned by
    trial.
  * decode reads per-pod vllm:kv_cache_usage_perc, already a fraction of
    capacity, so the threshold is compared to it directly.

Overlays follow the <strategy>/<topology> layout of the sibling
keda-epp-saturation guide, with base/k8s/ocp for both topologies:

  * optimized-baseline/ — co-located (kv_both): ONE ScaledObject carrying
    both triggers, KEDA scaling the single Deployment to the max of their
    desired replica counts.
  * pd-disaggregation/ — one ScaledObject per role, so prefill and decode
    scale independently.

Neither topology needs an EPP change: both base guides already register
inflight-load-producer and prefix-cache-affinity-filter in their shipped
router values. The only EPP-side work is setting peakPrefillThroughput to
a locally calibrated value, which the guide covers in Prerequisites.

Three query details are load-bearing and documented inline:

  * The prefill query intersects inflight_tokens with
    per_endpoint_queue_size on a derived target_pod label. inflight_tokens
    is a GaugeVec whose series are not deleted when an endpoint goes away,
    so a scaled-down pod strands a non-zero series and the sum never falls
    — the fleet would scale up but never back down. The queue-size
    collector is rebuilt from live endpoints every scrape, so the
    intersection admits only live pods.
  * Both triggers use sum(), not avg() or max(). With metricType
    AverageValue the HPA computes ceil(value / threshold), so the numerator
    must grow with the pool; a per-pod average cannot exceed ~1.0 and would
    pin the Deployment at 2 replicas.
  * `or vector(0)` only collapses to one series when the left side has an
    empty label set, which sum() guarantees. Without it the result keeps
    its pod labels, `or` appends a second {} series, and KEDA fails with
    FailedGetExternalMetric.

The ocp overlays reuse recipes/autoscaling/metrics-reader for Thanos
bearer auth and give the cluster-scoped ClusterRoleBinding a
namespace-unique name so deployments do not collide across namespaces or
across the guides sharing that recipe.

Also lists the new path in the workload-autoscaling README (Paths section
and the Choosing a Scaling Signal table).

Signed-off-by: Abhishek Malvankar <asm582@nyu.edu>

* docs: fix token-aware guide defects found on a Kind cluster

Addresses three defects and two documentation gaps found by deploying the
optimized-baseline path end to end against llm-d-inference-sim on a GPU-less
Kind cluster with KEDA 2.20.2, then driving it through a full scale-up to the
replica cap and back down. Each fix was reproduced and re-verified against a
live KEDA 2.20.2 apiserver.

Verify step two matched nothing and exited 1. `kubectl describe hpa | grep -A2
"External metric"` can never match: kubectl labels those rows "(target average
value)" and writes "external metric" only in lower case, inside the
FailedGetExternalMetric message. So the pattern matched only when the HPA was
broken and printed nothing when it was healthy — inverted, and silently so,
which is the precise failure mode the surrounding prose warns about. Replaced
with `kubectl get hpa`, which cannot produce empty output, rather than a
repaired pattern. Case-insensitive matching is not a fix for the same reason.

The run also surfaced a better diagnostic than the guide had, now documented: a
numeric left-hand value in the HPA's TARGETS column means the query resolved
and the pool is idle, whereas `<unknown>` means the trigger did not evaluate at
all — the state KEDA otherwise reports only as an HPA condition while serving
fallback replicas.

pollingInterval: 15 was inert in all three ScaledObjects. KEDA honours it only
when it owns activation or caching — minReplicaCount: 0, idleReplicaCount: 0,
or a trigger with useCachedMetrics — so every apply raised "PollingInterval is
configured but is not relevant", and with minReplicaCount: 1 the HPA's own sync
period governs instead. Removed, with a comment recording where responsiveness
is actually tuned and the conditions under which the field would start
mattering. Removal was preferred over adding useCachedMetrics because it
documents the behaviour that already exists rather than changing it.

The expected-output block no longer matched kubectl. KEDA 2.20 prints twelve
columns for `get scaledobject`, and the generated HPA renders
`0/1.500 (avg), 0/800m (avg)` rather than `0/1500m, 0/800m`. Both blocks now
carry output captured from a live cluster.

Two gaps the run exposed:

  * The "How offered load becomes a replica count" table assumes open-loop
    arrivals. Under closed-loop load inflight_tokens settles at
    concurrency x ISL and is invariant to capacity, so the prefill trigger
    climbs to maxReplicaCount by construction and stays there. Documented,
    together with the evenly-spread per-endpoint values that distinguish this
    from a stuck metric.

  * The OpenShift-versus-generic split had no slot for generic Kubernetes with
    an unauthenticated Prometheus, which is a common in-cluster development
    setup. Documented how to drop the authenticationRef blocks and the
    TriggerAuthentication, including why the higher trigger index must be
    removed first.

feat(guides): add Kueue-based replica rebalancing to workload-autoscaling (#2458)

* feat(guides): add Kueue-based replica rebalancing

Adds a second Features path to the workload-autoscaling guide that enforces a
shared GPU budget across model deployments with Kueue instead of a control loop
over HPAs.

Each model gets a ClusterQueue with a guaranteed GPU floor, all in one cohort,
and the `deployment` integration turns every replica pod into a Workload that is
admitted only when quota is free. Enforcement therefore happens below the HPA on
the pods it creates: the HPA needs no annotation, KEDA keeps sole ownership of
the HPA it generates, an idle model's GPUs are lent to a busy one, and a model
reclaims its floor by preemption. Over-budget demand becomes gated Pending pods
rather than a lowered maxReplicas.

The guide assumes the experimental replica rebalancer is uninstalled rather than
carrying steps to disable it: the two enforce the same budget from opposite sides
of the HPA and must never run together.

- guides/workload-autoscaling/kueue-rebalancing/{guide.yaml,README.md}, rendered
  by scripts/guide.py, with the install, opt-in, verification and cleanup steps
- optimized-baseline/base: ResourceFlavor, two ClusterQueues in a cohort with
  reclaimWithinCohort, and one LocalQueue per model (v1beta2)
- CI: install-kueue-crds.sh plus a step in the guide dry-run job, so the quota
  overlay is kustomize-built and server dry-run like every other overlay

* docs(guides): drop the replica rebalancer comparison table

The Kueue guide stands on its own; the side-by-side comparison with the

Signed-off-by: Abhishek Malvankar <asm582@nyu.edu>

* fix(guides): confine Kueue to the model namespace and opt in via the pod template

Review feedback on the Kueue rebalancing guide surfaced two problems that a run
against a live cluster confirmed, plus one that only showed up when the guide's
own commands were executed in order.

Confine Kueue to the model namespace. With the chart's default values the `pod`
integration is on and every webhook inherits `managedJobsNamespaceSelector`, so
`mpod.kb.io` intercepts pod CREATE in every namespace but `kube-system` and
`kueue-system`, with `failurePolicy: Fail`. Add kueue.values.yaml, which names
the model namespace in that selector, and install the chart with it. The knob is
inside `controllerManagerConfigYaml`, a single string Helm replaces rather than
merges, so the file repeats the 0.19.1 defaults verbatim.

Opt in on the pod template, not the Deployment. Kueue's `vdeployment` webhook
treats `metadata.labels[kueue.x-k8s.io/queue-name]` on a Deployment as immutable
once `status.readyReplicas > 0`, and rejects removing it at any replica count, so
patching a serving model server fails outright and cleanup cannot undo it. Label
`spec.template.metadata.labels` instead: each replica pod becomes its own
Workload through the `pod` integration, and the label can be patched back out.
The Deployment-level label remains the right choice at install time, which the
README now shows as a kustomize patch on the decode Deployment.

Order the deploy steps so the opt-in rollout can finish. The opt-in patch changes
the pod template, and at full quota the default `maxSurge: 25%` surge pod has no
GPU to claim: Kueue gates it and `kubectl rollout status` never returns. Set
`spec.strategy` first - that patch does not touch the pod template, so it rolls
nothing - then opt in.

Also: prefix the cluster-scoped queue names with `llm-d-` and stamp them with a
common label so verification can select them; move the LocalQueue namespace into
kustomization.yaml; assert in verify that each ClusterQueue is Active and still
in its cohort, instead of printing status that exits 0 either way; document the
Red Hat build of Kueue for OpenShift; and record the one-way Deployment label
under Limitations.

Where one patch applies to both model servers, `kubectl patch` takes both names

written out - one patch and one rollout wait per model, so a third model is a

The patch bodies switch from JSON to the flow-YAML form `kubectl patch` also
accepts, which drops a line of backslash-escaped quotes and lets the queue name

The two verification loops become single jq expressions over the whole

never production-ready and was explicitly limited to test and development
clusters. It also could not work with KEDA-generated HPAs, which own the
`maxReplicas` field it patches, so it did not compose with the recommended
autoscaling path. The Kueue-based guide enforces the same shared GPU budget
below the HPA and supersedes it.

described or compared against it:

  workload-autoscaling README. With one feature left, the `Features`
  wrapper heading is flattened into a single section.
- Rewrites the Kueue guide intro, prerequisites, `Perceived Effects` table,
  and contention section so they stand on their own instead of contrasting
  with the removed rebalancer. The prerequisite about a hard
  `requests.nvidia.com/gpu` ResourceQuota is kept, since a gated pod still
  counts against a ResourceQuota regardless of what created it.

fix(scripts): lint-envvars.py always exited 0, silently disabling the pre-commit/CI gate (#2416)

* fix(scripts): lint-envvars.py always exited 0, silently disabling the gate

main() printed undeclared-variable errors but then unconditionally
called sys.exit(0), so both the pre-commit hook and the CI
'pre-commit' job (.github/workflows/ci-pr-checks.yaml) always
reported success regardless of findings. Its sibling
lint-dockerfile-envvars.py already exits 1 on failure, and

exit 0 was a bug, not the intended behavior.

Also fixes a companion detection gap: find_locally_defined_vars only
matched assignments anchored at the very start of a line, so a
'case' arm one-liner like:
    linux/arm64) export SCCACHE_SERVER_UDS="..." ;;
was never recognized as a local definition, producing a false
'undeclared variable' report.

* docs(docker): declare env vars left undocumented while lint-envvars.py was a no-op

With the lint-envvars.py exit-code bug fixed, running it for real
over docker/scripts/**/*.sh surfaces the following pre-existing gaps
that had been accumulating silently since the check never actually
failed a build:

- build-uccl.sh: TARGETOS, VIRTUAL_ENV (used, never declared)
- build-nixl.sh, build-nvshmem.sh, build-ucx.sh: MAX_JOBS (used to
  parallelize the build, never declared)
- install-vllm.sh: CUDA_MINOR, FLASHINFER_VERSION,
  NVSHMEM_BUILD_FROM_SOURCE, VLLM_CHERRYPICK_{1,2}[_REMOTE],
  VLLM_SETUPTOOLS_SCM_PRETEND_VERSION (the last is only referenced
